c.tagline: A UNESCO-listed Saharan oasis of five fortified ochre-and-white M'Zab valley towns
langs: French (widely used in business and signage)

card: Rarely accepted outside major hotels; cash is essential throughout the M'Zab valley

taxi.fare: Negotiated flat rate, as meters are uncommon
taxi.fareNote: Agree the fare before departure; hiring a taxi with a local guide for the day is common for touring the five ksour

emergency.note: Dial 17 for police and 14 for medical/fire emergencies; English is rarely spoken by dispatchers, French is more useful

religion: Islam (Sunni majority, with a significant Ibadi Muslim community distinctive to the M'Zab valley)
walk: Each of the five ksour (walled towns) is walkable on its own steep, maze-like streets, but distances between them require a taxi or car

safety.safety: Generally safe for visitors traveling with a local guide, though Algeria's south requires more planning than typical tourist destinations
safety.crime: Violent crime against tourists is rare; the bigger practical challenges are limited English, cash-only transactions, and conservative local customs to respect (modest dress, guide requirements in Beni Isguen)

hood_landmark.Ghardaïa Medina: The 10th-century Ghardaïa Mosque and its pyramidal minaret
hood_landmark.Beni Isguen: Beni Isguen's strictly preserved walled old town
hood_landmark.Melika: Melika's hilltop cemetery overlooking the valley
hood_landmark.El Atteuf: El Atteuf's ancient mosque, an architectural precursor to modernist design

avoid.reason: There are no true no-go zones, but the holy walled town of Beni Isguen is entry-restricted — non-residents must enter with a local guide, photography of people is forbidden, and it closes to outsiders at prayer times.

Be discreet with cameras (locals, especially Mozabite women, must not be photographed) and keep valuables secure in the souk; check current conditions given past communal tensions in the M'zab valley.

hood_desc: The largest and richest of the five M'Zab towns, with the main market, mosque, and most hotels; the practical base for exploring the valley.
The most conservative and best-preserved of the five ksour, still closing its gates to non-residents at night; visits require a local guide.
A smaller hilltop town known for its panoramic cemetery and sweeping views over the whole M'Zab valley.
One of the smaller, quieter ksour with a compact fortified core, less visited than Ghardaïa or Beni Isguen.
The oldest of the five towns, its 11th-century mosque cited as an influence on modernist architect Le Corbusier.

water.note: Drink bottled water; tap water in the Saharan south is not reliable for visitors.

transit.sys: Local shared taxis and minibuses connecting the five ksour towns
transit.hours: Roughly daylight hours; travel after dark is uncommon
transit.map: Not centrally published; hotels and guides arrange transport between towns
transit.note: Alcohol is not sold locally (Beni Isguen and much of the valley is dry); a licensed local guide is required to enter Beni Isguen's old town

transport.air: Noumérat - Moufdi Zakaria Airport (GHA), serving Ghardaïa with domestic flights from Algiers
transport.train: No passenger rail service to Ghardaïa
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect Ghardaïa to Algiers (roughly 6-7 hr) and other southern Algerian towns
transport.car: The N1 highway connects Ghardaïa to Algiers; a guide or organized tour is recommended for independent travelers

net.m: Moderate 3G/4G coverage in town, weaker in the surrounding desert
net.w: Wifi available in hotels but often slow
net.gb: ~$5-10 for a prepaid tourist SIM (foreign registration can require passport and patience)
net.fwn: Wifi available in most hotels, though connection quality varies
net.ap: A Mobilis or Djezzy prepaid SIM, registered with your passport

tip.s: 10% is appreciated for local guides, required for entry to Beni Isguen
tip.r: Rounding up or 5-10% is appreciated, not obligatory

food.name: Couscous (ouchou)
food.desc: Hand-rolled semolina steamed over a broth of lamb, chickpeas, pumpkin and carrot. The M'zab version is soupier and sweeter than northern Algerian couscous.

places.name: Taqimit N Tizafri
places.note: Traditional Mozabite restaurant built around couscous varieties and chorba; set price per head.

places.name: Hotel El Djanoub restaurant
places.note: Hotel dining room that serves the full Friday-style couscous to non-guests.

places.name: Ghardaia souk eateries
places.note: Simple upstairs dining rooms around the market arcades cook couscous at lunchtime.

food.name: Chakhchoukha
food.desc: Thin flatbread torn into shreds and soaked in a spiced tomato, chickpea and lamb stew until it swells - a celebration dish eaten from a shared platter.

places.name: Taqimit N Tizafri
places.note: Mozabite and Algerian specialities cooked the long way, including the torn-bread stews.

places.name: Ghardaia souk eateries
places.note: Local canteens off the square serve chakhchoukha on the days they make bread.

places.name: Hotel Les Rostemides
places.note: Long-established hotel restaurant with a rotating menu of Algerian classics.

food.name: Berkoukes
food.desc: Large hand-rolled semolina pellets, somewhere between pasta and couscous, simmered in a meat and vegetable sauce - the M'zab valley's cold-night staple.

places.name: Taqimit N Tizafri
places.note: One of the few restaurants that cooks berkoukes rather than leaving it to home kitchens.

places.name: Ghardaia souk eateries
places.note: Ask at the market canteens - berkoukes often appears as the day's single dish.

places.name: Palm-grove guesthouses
places.note: Family-run oasis guesthouses serve berkoukes as a set evening meal for visitors.

food.name: Chorba frik
food.desc: Tomato and lamb broth thickened with green cracked wheat, mint and coriander, served scalding hot - the first thing on the table at any Algerian meal.

places.name: Taqimit N Tizafri
places.note: Chorba is the standard opener to its Mozabite set menus.

places.name: Ghardaia souk eateries
places.note: Cheap bowls of chorba with bread, especially around sunset in Ramadan.

places.name: Hotel El Djanoub restaurant
places.note: Reliable version if you want a quieter, sit-down setting away from the market.

food.name: Mechoui
food.desc: Whole lamb or shoulder roasted slowly over embers or in a pit until the skin crackles, carved and eaten with bread and salt - Saharan feasting food.

places.name: Grill stalls near Ghardaia bus station
places.note: Charcoal grills turning lamb through the afternoon; order by weight.

places.name: Palm-grove guesthouses
places.note: Arrange a mechoui a day ahead and it is roasted in the garden for the table.

places.name: Hotel Les Rostemides
places.note: Does grilled and roast lamb for groups; the safest bet without advance notice.

food.name: Deglet Nour dates
food.desc: Translucent amber dates from the M'zab palm groves, honeyed and almost transparent when held to the light - the valley's most famous export.

places.name: Beni Isguen date market
places.note: The valley's celebrated auction market, where dates are sold by the crate each afternoon.

places.name: Ghardaia souk
places.note: Date sellers under the arcades will let you taste several varieties before buying.

places.name: Palm-grove smallholdings
places.note: Growers sell direct from the groves in the autumn harvest season.

food.name: Mint tea
food.desc: Green tea boiled hard with sugar and a fistful of fresh mint, poured from height into small glasses. Ghardaia is dry and conservative - this is the social drink.

places.name: Ghardaia souk tea houses
places.note: Cafes under the market arcades pour tea all day; the best people-watching in the valley.

places.name: Taqimit N Tizafri
places.note: Meals close with mint tea and dates in the traditional Mozabite way.

places.name: Melika hilltop cafes
places.note: Small terraces looking across the valley to Ghardaia - tea with the best view.

food.name: Lben
food.desc: Cool, slightly sour churned buttermilk drunk straight from the bowl to cut the heat and the spice - the desert's oldest thirst-quencher.

places.name: Ghardaia souk dairy sellers
places.note: Sold by the bottle from coolers in the market alongside fresh cheese.

places.name: Palm-grove guesthouses
places.note: Served with the evening meal, often from the household's own goats.

places.name: El Atteuf village shops
places.note: The oldest of the five ksour; village shops keep lben and raib chilled.

landmarks: Ksar of Ghardaïa and the Great Mosque
The largest of the UNESCO-listed M'zab hill towns spirals in earthen tiers toward its stark pyramid-shaped minaret, a thousand-year-old Mozabite masterpiece.
Beni Isguen
The M'zab's holy city, entered only with a local guide, preserves strict traditions, a daily auction market and immaculate whitewashed lanes behind fortified walls.
Ghardaïa Market Square (Place du Marché)
Arcaded and ochre-hued, this lively souk square trades carpets, dates and copperware beneath the gaze of the old town rising behind.
El Atteuf (Ksar of El Atteuf)
The oldest M'zab settlement, founded in 1012, whose fluid whitewashed Sidi Brahim mosque famously inspired Le Corbusier's chapel at Ronchamp.
Sidi Brahim Mosque
This ancient, organically curved prayer hall in El Atteuf, with its low arches and sculpted openings, is a landmark of Saharan vernacular architecture.
Bounoura
Perched on a rocky spur above the wadi, this fortified ksar of golden lanes and watchtowers is among the most photogenic of the five M'zab cities.
Melika
A hilltop ksar known for the whitewashed tomb complex of Sidi Aïssa and panoramic views over the entire M'zab valley.
The M'zab Palm Groves
Thousands of date palms fill the wadi beneath the ksour, irrigated by an ingenious centuries-old water-sharing system and dotted with summer houses.
Tafilelt (Tafilelt Tajdit)
A striking modern eco-ksar completed in the 2000s, proving Mozabite urban traditions alive by housing thousands in sustainable desert architecture.
Ghardaïa Panoramic Viewpoint
From the rocky heights above town, the five ksour, palm groves and desert plateau compose one of the Sahara's most extraordinary urban landscapes.

train.note: There is no passenger railway to Ghardaïa - SNTF's network (https://www.sntf.dz/) serves the northern coastal belt and the line south to Djelfa, stopping well short of the M'zab valley. Arrive by coach on the Trans-Saharan highway or fly into Noumérat airport.

bus.note: No international coaches - Ghardaïa is 600 km into the Sahara and the southern borders are closed or heavily restricted. SNTV and private operators run from the Ghardaïa terminal north to Algiers in about 8-9 hours and south toward El Goléa and Tamanrasset, a journey of two days. Buy at the terminal in cash.

ferry.note: Ghardaïa sits in the M'zab valley deep in the northern Sahara with no water at all, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Metlili & Sebseb Oasis
half.blurb: Chaamba nomad town and palm oasis south of Ghardaïa, known for camel rides and traditional Saharan tea.

full.name: El Goléa
full.blurb: Desert oasis town with dense palm groves and a hilltop ruined citadel, about three hours south of Ghardaïa.
